newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West pushes on landmines but China says phased ban.
newsitem.headline: West pushes on landmines but China says phased ban.

text.p: Western diplomats said on Thursday they still hoped for last-minute success in naming a special coordinator who would try to launch negotiations on landmines at the Conference on Disarmament.
But Syria and other non-aligned countries including Cuba may hold up reaching consensus again at the United Nations-backed forum, which ends its current session on Friday, they added.
China's ambassador Sha Zukang took the floor to argue in favour of negotiating a landmines ban in phases, but said he would not object to naming a special coordinator on the issue.

The weapons remained an "indispensable, legitimate and conventional means of national defense" for his vast country which has long land borders and an "uncertain security environment", according to Beijing's envoy.
"China is in favour of imposing strict and feasible restrictions on anti-personnel landmines and their use, thereby achieving the objective of an ultimate ban in a step-by-step manner," Sha said.
"In short, China is not opposed to the objective of (the) prohibition of anti-personnel landmines realised in a phased approach, but cannot agree to any immediate total ban," he said.

The 61-member talks have been deadlocked all year due to a row between Western states eager to negotiate global bans on landmines and production of bomb-making fissile material, and non-aligned states seeking greater elimination of nuclear arms.

A special coordinator would seek consensus to launch negotiations on a global accord which would ban the use, storage, production and transfer of landmines. The weapons are blamed for causing 25,000 deaths a year, mainly civilians.
"It would appear that Syria is the only one objecting," a senior Western diplomat told Reuters.
"I am not optimistic. There may be something tomorrow (Friday)," she added.

The weekly plenary on Thursday looked set to continue for hours, with a lengthy list of speakers wanting to go on record before the talks recess for a month. The talks reconvene on July 28 for the final seven-week session of the year.
Some 26 non-aligned countries including India and Mexico have tabled a work programme which would set up a committee to seek total elimination of nuclear weapons within a fixed period.
But the five declared nuclear weapon states (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) categorically reject such demands for negotiations in Geneva on total disarmament.
Hisami Kurokochi, Japan's ambassador who has ended her term, summed up frustration shared by many in her final speech.
"I must express my deep regret that the CD, since the beginning of this year, has not started substantial work on any of the issues on our agenda," she said.

Using the occasion to criticise excessive use of the forum's rule that decisions be taken by consensus, Kurokochi urged: "When a point at issue is a procedural matter which does not prejudge the question of substance, every country should refrain as much as possible from exercising a veto.
"The most important thing is not to make the CD a captive to the linkage strategy because it will deny progress in the CD."

Germany's envoy Guenther Seibert agreed: "The events during this session have demonstrated again the self-defeating effects of holding progress in one area hostage to progress in other areas. Linkages are a recipe for blocking any kind of progress in the CD and should be discarded...

"This is a critical year for the conference. The successes of the recent past constrast with our inability today to reach agreement on the new issues to be negotiated," said New Zealand's envoy Wade Armstrong.
"We are facing a stalemate in our substantive work. We have not been able to untangle the Gordian Knot."
